content.thinking:
I'm sizing the red panda realistically—roughly 60cm body length with a long tail—and planning to pose it balanced on a mossy stone about 35cm tall, with its tail curved up in an S-shape for visual interest.

Landing on a quadruped stance with all four paws on the stone but legs spread wide for stability, tail arcing high as a counterweight. I'll give it one forepaw lightly raised for a touch of charm, keeping the rig simple while aiming for a bright, clean cel-shaded Genshin-style look.

For accessories, I'm thinking a small gold-trimmed ribbon or scarf with tassels, a jade bell charm hanging from the collar, and a glowing Dendro-style motif carved into a mossy stone nearby. The coloring should follow real red panda markings — cream ears with white tufts, brown tear lines, white cheeks and eyebrow spots, rust-red back, dark belly and legs, and a ringed tail — while the eyes get an anime-style upgrade with a warm amber iris.

Now I'm working out the layout: a central boulder built from a low-poly flattened sphere with mottled stone and moss paint, topped with a green mossy cap, positioned at the origin with the model facing forward.

I'm adding extra decoration to the stone — moss tufts, ferns, mushrooms, small scattered pebbles, and some glowing green-cyan motes for a Dendro-style magical touch, plus a gold-trimmed engraved rune for a bit of ornamentation. I'm sizing the boulder so the panda's wide stance mostly covers its base, keeping the whole composition feeling balanced and stable.

Now I'm working out the stone's geometry: I need it to sit with a flat bottom on the floor while having its top surface at the right height for the paws, so a sphere scaled into an ellipsoid sinks too far below ground — I'm switching to an icosahedron with flat shading instead to get a flatter base.

I'll build the rock using a lathe profile tracing an irregular outline from axis center outward to about 0.44 radius then up to 0.35 height, giving a faceted asymmetric stone when revolved with low segment count. To break the lathe's inherent symmetry I'm scaling it slightly along one axis and scattering a few smaller overlapping boulder chunks around the base for natural irregularity, bringing the rock top to roughly 0.33 units, which sets up the panda's shoulder and head heights stacked above it.

Now I'm thinking the stone should be sized like a round boulder about 0.5 wide and 0.4 deep for the panda to balance on, with its paws planted in a stance roughly 0.14 apart front-to-back and 0.14 side-to-side, plus small decorative elements like clovers, mushrooms, pebbles, and grass tufts scattered on the ground around the base for composition. Next I'm laying out the animal's skeleton joints -- hips as root, spine segments, chest, neck, head, jaw, ears, and tail -- to prepare for rigging the pose.

For proportions, I'm going with a cute chibi red panda: low-slung and quadrupedal with slightly longer hind legs, a big round head with wide cheeks, a short snout, and large triangular ears. Now I'm working out specific coordinates for the body sitting on the stone's flattened top, positioning the spine from hips to shoulders with a thick fluffy body radius, and sizing the short hind legs from hip down to paw.

Setting up the leg chain structure...

Setting up spine coordinates...

Now mapping the neck from base up to a forward head position, sizing the skull and snout with cream muzzle and black nose, then starting the tail curve from the rump outward into an S-shape.

Writing tail paint shader...

I'm also reconsidering tail length against the body scale, trimming the point sequence down since a 1.1m sweep reads too long for a stylized 0.5m body.

For the legs, I'm weighing lifted versus planted forepaws—a raised paw adds personality but a symmetrical planted stance is safer for rigging. Given the "balancing" story concept, I'll go with both forepaws planted symmetrically, tail and head up, with small variations like splayed paws and one hind foot set slightly back for naturalism.

Now I'm reconsidering the stone itself—making it smaller so the panda's paws grip near its edges would heighten the sense of precarious balance. I'm sketching paw positions and comparing them against the stone's footprint radius, deciding to narrow the top of the stone (asymmetric radius in x versus z) rather than keeping it wide, so the pose feels more tense and unstable.

I'll flatten the top profile and let the paws sink slightly below the stone's surface so they look embedded rather than floating. For texture, I'm setting up a paint function that applies a mottled grey-blue stone color with patches of saturated green moss draping over the top, using noise and height-based thresholds to decide where moss appears versus bare rock.

Adding a gold rune detail now: I want a glowing green Dendro-style glyph ring decaled onto the front face of the stone, so I'll generate it as an SVG texture and apply it with a glow effect layered onto the curved surface.

For accessories, I'm planning a Genshin-inspired palette (Dendro green, gold, ivory, teal, panda rust) with a teal collar loop around the neck edged in gold stitching, plus a hanging gold leaf-shaped pendant holding a glowing green gem and a small bell, finished off with a tasseled strand built from small capsule shapes.

I'm also adding a small gold ear clip with a tiny tassel, a handful of glowing dendro-seed spheres orbiting near the tail, and head details like pale eyebrow marks, cheek tufts, and painted tear marks typical of a red panda's face.

Now I'm defining the skull's fur coloring: rust on top and outside of ears fading to cream on cheeks and muzzle, with a black nose, dark eye rings, and rust tear-mark stripes running from the eye corners down to the mouth, plus white-cream ear interiors with tufted rims.

Adding tear-mark coloring...

I'll build the coat with furEdge wrapping a subtly mottled back color against the belly tone, letting cel shading pick shadow tones automatically. Legs get a dark brownish-black with cel shading and cream claws, and I'm planning fur card tufts (flame-shaped, ink-edged) for cheeks, chest, tail, and ears.

For the tuft cards, I'll draw them in greyscale and tint using the coat paint evaluated at each card's root normal, so cel shading still applies naturally. I'll scatter these cards along the tail sweep to build a fluffy silhouette, using four-triangle cards for efficiency across roughly 400 instances.

Now I'm working out facial features: amber-brown anime-style eyes with amber iris, light highlight, and dark edge tones, placed at an angle on the skull sphere, plus dark eye patches typical of red pandas. For the nose, I'm making a black rounded shape with a small white highlight sphere.

For the mouth, I'm deciding on a simple closed ink mouth line rather than an open smile with tongue/teeth, keeping things simpler, with a separate cream-colored jaw piece and muzzle shape. I'm defining the head joint position and orientation relative to the neck, setting up local axes for the forward-facing bone.

Now I'm computing the skull sphere's center position and dimensions in model space, slightly offset forward and up from the head joint, with squashed radii for a low-poly stylized shape.

Next I'm placing the snout as a cream-colored sphere offset from the skull center, adding a small wide nose sphere at the tip, and sketching out a lower jaw capsule joint beneath the snout.

For cheek fur, I'm weighing options — spiky cone tufts pointing outward versus scattered fur-texture cards filtered to the cheek region using position checks on the skull surface — leaning toward cheap scattered cards for a cost-effective ruff effect.

Now I'm designing the ears: large upright triangular red panda ears, wide-set on top of the head, rust-colored outside with a white rim and cream fluffy interior, built from extruded rounded-triangle outlines with joints placed above and behind the head center, angled outward and slightly forward.

I'm working out how the inner ear decoration should be oriented differently from the outer ear so its coloring reads correctly from front and back, trying different axis conventions to keep the thickness direction consistent with the outline's forward-facing side.

Confirming the inner ear face stays hidden behind the outer one, then I move to orienting the ear's up-vector with a slight outward and forward lean so it reads as natural ear tilt. I'm defining the ear outline as a rounded triangle shape with specific base width and height measurements anchored at the ear joint bone.

I'll paint cream tips with a zigzag edge against the rust base, then add a gold ring and dangling tassel ornament to the left ear. I'm also thinking about overall body proportions, a darker chest bib, and planning front legs as shoulder-elbow-paw segments bending backward like a knee.

For hind legs I'm going with thigh and shin segments bending forward at the knee, since red pandas are plantigrade with short stubby limbs, working out joint lengths so the bent reach matches the hip-to-foot distance.

Now I'm designing the paws themselves: a flattened foot pad as an ellipsoid plus four small toe bumps fanned out front, and deciding whether to give each toe its own joint for more natural posing, which would add sixteen extra joints across all four paws.

I'm tallying up the full skeleton — hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, ears, tail, legs, and toes — landing around 45 joints total, which feels manageable. For the body mesh, I'm planning to sweep separate geometry along the spine chain and neck chain rather than one continuous path, accepting some overlap at the neck-chest junction since it'll be hidden under the cheek ruff anyway.

Now I'm working out actual coordinates: placing the hips/pelvis root, figuring out how a 4-point path yields 3 spans and joints, and positioning the rump cap and tail base just behind the pelvis to match a realistic red panda proportions of roughly half a meter body length.

I'm sizing the body radii along the spine (fuller at the rump, tapering slightly toward the chest) and deciding where to scatter small fluff tufts — chest ruff, cheeks, tail edge, leg-back, and ear tufts — keeping the clean Genshin aesthetic by using them sparingly. Now I'll start translating all these coordinates into actual code, making sure the stone perch properly supports the legs.

For the tail, I'm planning alternating russet and buff rings along its length using a zigzag edge pattern, with a darker cap near the tip, picking colors that fit the warm red panda palette and work with the cel-shading hue shift.

I'm varying the tail's thickness so it's slimmer at the base, thicker through the middle, and tapered at the tip, with rounded caps, then scattering small tuft cards along the sweep that pick up the same paint coloring as the tail. Beyond the tail, I'm now placing extra ground details like moss-covered stones near the front-right of the scene and adding mushrooms via a lathe shape.

I'm adding a few cream-stemmed, teal-capped mushrooms with spotted bases, card-based fern fronds, clover and grass cards, and a small glowing dendro leaf emblem. I'm also scattering a few gold-centered five-petal flowers, draping moss fringe cards around the stone's rim to hang downward, and placing a ground disc beneath everything as the base the model stands on.

Now I'm sizing a round turf base roughly 0.6 radius and thin, with an irregular grassy outline and mottled cel-shaded paint so the stone sits naturally on it like a small diorama, keeping proportions sensible against the creature's tail trailing behind it.

For decoration, I'm planning a gold-trimmed rune circle on the stone's front face — splitting it into two separate decals set slightly apart so the gold filigree ring stays unlit while the inner glyph glows, avoiding the whole emblem looking uniformly bright.

Now I need to figure out exact placement on the stone surface, using a point and direction to project the decal onto the front-left face where it's visible from the camera's three-quarter view.

For floating seeds, I'm scattering small glowing octahedrons near the tail and panda, keeping heights below the tail top. For the collar, I'm sweeping a teal loop around the neck joint with a pendant hanging at the chest, positioned where the head meets the body.

Actually I reconsider the collar placement — rather than the neck, I'll loop it lower around the shoulder area near the spine's chest joint, checking that the plane doesn't accidentally cut through the legs positioned at either side.

For the scarf geometry itself, I'll treat it as a flat ribbon swept along the body path with a wider, thin cross-section rather than a simple round tube, possibly adding thin gold trim along each edge of the teal ribbon.

For accessories, I'm planning a decorative knot near the front-right of the neck with two hanging ribbon tails that taper into forked ends with tassels, plus a pendant with a gold frame holding a glowing green jade gem. I need to figure out exactly where to anchor these to the neck surface so the ribbon tails hang naturally down the chest.

I'm figuring out the exact placement of a flat ribbon against the sloped chest surface, raycasting from the front to find the correct z-offset so it sits just outside the body mesh, plus adding a small gold bell pendant below it. Now I'm ready to move into actual code, carefully checking the API usage to avoid type errors, and I'll need some texture assets for any card elements too.

I'm designing simple tinted SVG textures: a generic white tuft shape reusable for cheeks and other fur patches via color tinting, plus green moss, fern frond, and grass blade cards for foliage detailing, all sharing one 1024 texture atlas to keep things efficient.

Now I'm working out the stone surface shader, blending a mossy patch pattern using noise and surface normal plus height-based bias so moss appears more on upward-facing, lower areas, with the rest showing a cracked stone texture.

I'm also setting up a bright Genshin-style cel palette with lit and highlight variants for rust and belly tones to give the piece a more hand-painted feel.

Continuing to work through the color set: cream, tear, nose, teal scarf, gold accent with its own cel shadow, dendro glow greens, and stone/moss tones for shading. Keeping the flat color count under 64 since cel paints don't count against that limit, and considering whether gold reads better as a flat hex or a cel'd gradient.

Settling on cel shading applied consistently across all parts for visual coherence, and working out texture density—at 1024px atlas resolution the texel density comes out to roughly 1.4mm per texel for the painted area, which feels about right. Now starting on the skeleton code setup...

Importing the needed builder, paint, path, and toon-shading utilities, then trimming unused imports after the typecheck. Starting the root hip joint definition.

Now I'm building the spine chain using a catmull-rom curve through four points, verifying that the joint count matches the span count so there's no extra tip joint, and thinking through how the neck chain should parent off the end of spine3 toward the chest.

Next I'm laying out the neck's path forward from the spine's end point toward the head base, then placing the head joint at the neck's final point with a forward-facing direction so it sits naturally atop the neck.

For the tail, I'm defining a six-point chain extending backward from the hips with a gentle downward curve, naming the joints tail1 through tail6. Then I'm starting on the shoulder joints, looping over left and right sides to mirror the leg structure.

Now I'm calculating the front and hind limb geometry, computing paw target positions and segment lengths so the legs reach the ground plausibly with slight elbow bend.

I'm defining the leg sweep radii that taper from thigh to ankle, and sketching the paw as layered spheres sized to form a rounded foot shape.

I'm reconciling the stone's flat top height with the leg bottom so paws sit naturally on the surface, letting moss caps absorb the slight embedding. Now I'm laying out four toe positions spaced across the front of each paw.

Adding toe capsules and claw cones...

Moving on to the head, I'm starting the skull as a sphere with the face paint, then adding puffed cheek spheres on either side.

Sketching the mouth line...

Now I'm planning the rest of the accessories: scarf, pendant, tassels, ear ornaments, flowers, ferns, and mushrooms, thinking I'll just write them all out and iterate with a preview afterward. For flowers I'm picturing small flattened sphere petals arranged radially around a gold center, oriented outward like a simple blossom.

Writing SVG code...

Since the attachment sits at the drawing's bottom edge and the tip hangs down, I'm drawing shapes wide at the base narrowing to a point at the top, same approach for the fur tuft and moss lumps rendered as flattened mottled spheres.

For the base turf, I'm extruding an irregular blob outline in the XZ plane with a thin thickness centered around a small offset, using around ten angled points for a natural shape, then applying a mottled green paint pattern across it.

I'm deciding the top face stays painted flat regardless of orientation, adding a darker soil-brown stripe on the turf's side using a normal-based threshold, and skipping any extra filigree detail. For small rocks I'm using faceted icosahedron geometry scattered and sunk into the turf, painted with a continuous moss pattern based on position, while I'm still figuring out whether the lathe profile for the main stone supports a z-axis scale option.

Writing lathe geometry code...

Moss cushions will let the paws sink in nicely for a cozy look. Now I'm sketching the main build: setting up a seeded RNG for deterministic scatter, placing moss tufts and grass-textured cards across the stone surface with angle and size variation, then working out face paint placement using local head-space coordinates for positioning.

Writing face paint logic...

Deciding I'll skip ink lines except for mouth/eyelid. For the body, I'm defining a paint function giving a hard-edged lighter dorsal stripe versus rust sides, then applying cel shading with a fur-edge blend between back and belly colors, using normal thresholds to separate belly, sides, and dorsal regions with a toon-style outline.

For legs, I'm making them mostly dark brown with a rust patch near the upper thigh, using a position-based fur edge along the vertical axis to blend the coat color into the dark leg color at a specific height, with jagged teeth for a furry transition.

Then I'm wiring up the tail with its ring and tip colors, and the ear with its own cel-shaded paint, making sure each paint definition resolves correctly as nested color types.

Now I'm defining the jaw joint relative to the head, positioning and aiming it forward and down, then shaping the jaw itself as a small ellipsoid attached to the jaw bone's local coordinate frame.

Still working through positioning...

I realize for parts like the snout and jaw without explicit rotation, the geometry just uses world axes directly for width, height, and forward depth, which keeps things simple, while limbs needing specific orientation will use sweeps instead. I'm planning to create a helper function for ellipsoid parts that takes a center, radii, color, and bone to simplify building the rest of the body.

For the ears, I'm setting up joints parented to the head, positioned using local coordinates with left/right, up, and forward offsets, using a sign variable to mirror left and right ears symmetrically.

Writing extrude geometry...

I'm adding inner fluff tufts scattered near the front of the ear, then painting the inner ear with cream tones blending into a pinkish patch near the bottom center. Next I'm figuring out eyebrow and eye placement by computing azimuth angles from the skull center, placing eyes roughly 33 degrees off the front axis.

I'm sizing the eye decals fairly large for a chibi proportions, spacing them so there's a comfortable gap between the two eyes, then embedding small cream spheres for the brow spots using the stick helper with scaled dimensions along the surface normal.

Now I'm scattering tuft cards across the cheek puffs with outward-back flow direction, planning to skip mirroring since the tufts are symmetric, then moving to building the scarf by sweeping the neck geometry and setting up a loop perpendicular to the first neck bone segment.

I'm worried the neck loop might intersect the body since the neck starts inside the chest, so I should anchor it further along the neck path instead, maybe around the midpoint, and check how it reads in preview alongside the cheek ruffs. If the scarf ends up hidden, I might swap it for a ribbon bow with hanging tassels instead, then move on to placing a chest pendant and adding glow motes and dendro leaf sprouts.

A cute idea: a tiny two-leaf sprout glowing on the head between the ears, Nahida-style, in cel-shaded green with a glowing tip. I'm defining the color palette with cel-shaded gold and teal tones, and setting up the extrude bevel parameter to stay within the half-thickness limit, while using a surface helper for attaching parts to sweeps.

input.command: cd ~/tmp-archive/sonnet-100/redPandaSonnet/ && sed -n 60,140p src/ik.ts | head -5; sed -n 169,200p src/builder.ts; grep -n "scale" src/builder.ts | head -20; ls ~/tmp-archive/sonnet-100/redPandaSonnet/scratch
